name: SNT as Legal Person: The Body Extension Doctrine
author: Magistrate Yuki Fernandez-Okonkwo, GLMZ Administrative Tribunal
body:
The Body Extension Doctrine, established in the landmark case Tessera v. Olumide (2204), holds that any cybernetic implant bonded to a person's body through SNT is legally an extension of that person's body. It is not property. It is not a device. It is body.

The implications are sweeping:

ASSAULT: Forcibly removing or damaging an SNT-bonded implant constitutes assault on the person, not destruction of property. The charge is bodily harm, not vandalism. Sentencing reflects this.

THEFT: Stealing an implant that is SNT-bonded to a living person is not theft — it is aggravated assault with mutilation. The property classification does not apply because the implant is, legally, part of the victim's body.

REPOSSESSION: A creditor cannot repossess an SNT-bonded implant for unpaid debts. The Gradient Compact's prohibition on debtor imprisonment extends to debtor dismemberment. A corponation that financed an implant can pursue financial penalties but cannot forcibly reclaim the hardware once it is bonded.

This last point is the most contentious. Corponations that finance augmentation argue that the Body Extension Doctrine allows patients to default on augmentation loans with no meaningful recourse. The patient keeps the arm. The corponation absorbs the loss. In practice, corponations have responded by requiring SNT maintenance contracts as a condition of financing — if you stop paying, they don't take your arm, but they stop maintaining the bonding layer that keeps it functional. The arm dies on your body. You keep it. It just doesn't work.

This has been challenged in court. It has not been overturned. The distinction between 'we took your arm' and 'we stopped maintaining your arm' is the kind of legal fiction that corponation attorneys specialize in.
